reels.hook_b: You learned it before you had words for it.
cards: What did your house do with anger?
Shouting? Silence? Slammed doors? Nothing at all?
Now: what do you do with yours?
Most of what we inherit feels like personality.

reels.caption:
Every family has a way of handling anger, money, affection, conflict and failure. You learned yours before you could name it, which is why it feels like who you are.

Try this: write what your house did with each, then what you do now. Mark each one keep, return or not sure.

Which one would you return?

Practice: Moodius. Full essay "The Things We Inherit Without Realising" on the Substack, link in bio.
reels.first_comment: Anger, money, affection, conflict or failure: which one did your family handle worst?

reels.hook: You catch your father's sigh coming out of your own mouth.
reels.hook_b: The research on family patterns is darker and more hopeful than you'd think.
cards: You catch your father's sigh coming out of your own mouth.
Researchers have measured how strongly patterns pass down.
Even in the hardest cases, about two in three people didn't repeat them.
Review: Kaufman & Zigler, Am. J. Orthopsychiatry (1987)
What helped: someone in their corner, and an honest account of what happened.
Inherited isn't the same as sentenced.
Send it to someone breaking a pattern.

reels.caption:
In the most studied and hardest case, whether people who were maltreated as children go on to maltreat their own, a 1987 review estimated about one in three did. That's a real risk. It also means most didn't.

The people who broke the pattern tended to have someone supportive, a partner or an adult in childhood, and an honest, coherent account of what had happened to them.

What pattern are you breaking?

Evidence: Kaufman & Zigler (1987); Australian Institute of Family Studies review. Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.

carousel_caption:
The things we inherit most completely are the ones we never had a chance to look at.

Research on the hardest cases shows family patterns are real and measurable, and that most people don't simply repeat them. The ones who break a pattern tend to have support and an honest account of what happened.

Which of the five would you return?

Evidence: van IJzendoorn 1995 (meta-analysis); Kaufman & Zigler 1987 (review); AIFS review. Frameworks: Bowen, Jung (interpretive). Ezekiel 18:2 (KJV).
notes: A 1995 meta-analysis found that how parents talked about their own childhoods matched their babies' attachment patterns about 75% of the time. A strong link. But the obvious explanation, how responsive the parents were, accounted for only part of it. Researchers called the rest the 'transmission gap'. Something in between can change what's handed on.

Ezekiel quotes an old proverb: the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge. He quotes it to reject it. That tension, between what's handed down and the claim that we aren't bound by it, is where the research lands too.
Five words to write about tonight: anger, money, affection, conflict, failure. What did your house do with each? What do you do now? You'll find at least one you'd like to give back.
